---
title: "Quiz: kernel functions and the kernel trick"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A kernel function is $k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = \varphi(\mathbf x)\cdot\varphi(\mathbf z)$; the SVM's decision function is $f(\mathbf x) = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x) + b$.

---

**Q1.** Points inside a circle of radius 1 belong to one class, points in a ring around it to the other. Which single extra feature makes them linearly separable, and what is the separating plane?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What distinguishes the two classes?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The squared distance from the centre, $x_3 = x_1^2 + x_2^2$. The plane $x_3 = r^2$, with $r$ between the inner radius and the ring, separates them; in the original plane it is the circle of radius $r$.
:::

---

**Q2.** What is the "kernel trick", in one sentence? Why is it needed?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the SVM need from the data?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The SVM needs the data only through dot products, so every dot product $\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf x_j$ can be replaced by a kernel function $k(\mathbf x_i, \mathbf x_j)$ that equals a dot product in a lifted space, without ever computing the lifted features. It is needed because those spaces are huge (hundreds of coordinates for quadratic features of 20 inputs) or infinite (RBF).
:::

---

**Q3.** Compute $k(\mathbf x, \mathbf z) = (\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z + 1)^2$ for $\mathbf x = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf z = (2, 3)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One dot product, then add 1 and square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf z = 2$, so $k = 3^2 = 9$.
:::

---

**Q4.** An RBF SVM has $\gamma = 4$. What is its length scale? Two points 1 apart: what is their similarity?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Length scale $1/\sqrt\gamma$; similarity $e^{-\gamma d^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1/\sqrt4 = 0.5$. Similarity $e^{-4} = 0.018$: almost none.
:::

---

**Q5.** An RBF SVM has zero training errors and every training point is a support vector. What is probably wrong, and what do you change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far does one point's bump reach?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\gamma$ is too large (and $C$ large): each bump reaches only its own point, so the SVM memorises the training set with an island around every point: overfitting. Lower $\gamma$ (and possibly $C$), and choose both by cross-validation.
:::

---

**Q6.** What does an RBF SVM predict far away from all training points?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to every bump $e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x_i - \mathbf x\|^2}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All bumps vanish, so $f(\mathbf x) \to b$: the class given by the sign of $b$, with $|f|$ small (low confidence). The SVM has no information there; it does not extrapolate a trend.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is the RBF kernel function related to the contrast weights of graph cuts?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare $e^{-\gamma\|\mathbf x - \mathbf z\|^2}$ with $e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They are the same function of a distance: the graph-cut n-link weight is the RBF kernel function of the two grey levels with $\gamma = 1/(2\sigma^2)$. Both measure similarity; the matrix of all pairwise values is the SVM's kernel matrix and the affinity matrix of normalized cuts.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Which points have $\alpha_i > 0$ in the dual solution, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Complementary slackness: $\alpha_i\,(y_if(\mathbf x_i) - 1 + \xi_i) = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Only points whose margin constraint is tight: on the edge of the street ($y_if = 1$, $0 < \alpha_i \le C$) or, with a soft margin, inside it or on the wrong side ($\alpha_i = C$). For every point safely outside the street the constraint is slack, so its multiplier is 0: these are not support vectors and do not appear in $f$.
:::
